t.1.57.1: Then, O Rāma, having heard Triśaṅku's words, which were filled with anger, the hundred sons of the sage spoke this to the king.
t.1.57.2: O wicked-minded one, you have been rejected by your truth-speaking guru. How is it that, passing him over, you have come to another branch?
t.1.57.3: For the family priest is the supreme refuge of all the Ikṣvākus, and the word of one who speaks the truth cannot be transgressed.
t.1.57.4: And the blessed sage Vasiṣṭha said, "It is impossible. How indeed could we be able to accomplish that sacrifice of yours?"
t.1.57.5: You are foolish, best of men; let it be gone back to your own city once more. The revered one is capable of performing sacrifices even for the three worlds, O king.
t.1.57.6: Having heard those words of theirs, every syllable trembling with anger, the king once again spoke these words to them.
t.1.57.7: I have been rejected by my guru, and likewise by the sons of my guru. I shall go to another refuge; may it be well with you, O ascetics rich in austerity.
t.1.57.8: But the sons of the sage, hearing that speech so fraught with dreadful intent, became exceedingly enraged and cursed him: "You shall become a Caṇḍāla!" Having spoken thus, those great-souled ones entered their own hermitage.
t.1.57.10: Seeing him in the form of a Caṇḍāla, O Rāma, all the ministers, together with the citizens who had followed him, abandoned him and fled.
t.1.57.9: Then, when the night had passed, the king, having fallen to the state of a Caṇḍāla, became dark, wearing dark garments, rough, with dishevelled hair, smeared with unguents and garlands from the funeral pyre, and decked with ornaments of iron.
t.1.57.11: Then, O Kākutstha, a certain king of great self-mastery, burning day and night, went to Viśvāmitra, whose wealth was his austerity.
t.1.57.12: But the sage Viśvāmitra, O Rāma, seeing that king rendered fruitless and bearing the form of a Caṇḍāla, was moved to compassion.
t.1.57.13: Out of compassion, that supremely righteous one of great splendor spoke these words to the king of dreadful appearance: "Good fortune to you."
t.1.57.15: Then, having heard those words, the king who had become a caṇḍāla, skilled in speech, spoke with joined palms to the one who was a master of speech.
t.1.57.14: O prince of great strength, O heroic lord of Ayodhyā, you who have been reduced to the state of a caṇḍāla by a curse, what is the purpose of your coming?
t.1.57.16: I have been rejected by my preceptor, and likewise by my preceptor's sons. Without attaining that desire at all, I have met with its very reverse.
t.1.57.17: "May I go to heaven with my body": such was my cherished vision. A hundred sacrifices have been performed by me, and yet that fruit is not attained.
t.1.57.19: Sacrifices of many kinds have been performed, the subjects have been protected in accordance with dharma, and the great-souled elders have been gratified by good character and conduct.
t.1.57.18: Never before have I spoken an untruth, nor shall I ever speak one, even when I have fallen into hardships, O gentle one; by the dharma of a kṣatriya I swear this to you.
t.1.57.20: O bull among sages, though I strive in dharma and wish to perform a sacrifice, my preceptors are not satisfied with me.
t.1.57.21: I deem fate alone to be supreme, and human effort to be meaningless. Everything is overpowered by fate, for fate is indeed the ultimate recourse.
t.1.57.22: Blessings be upon you! You should grant your favour to me, who am deeply distressed, longing for your grace, and whose efforts have been thwarted by fate.
t.1.57.23: I shall go to no other refuge; there is no other shelter for me. You ought to turn back fate by your own human effort.
